items.stimulus:
Four people were asked what they think about progress and tradition.

Orla Vance, furniture maker: "A tradition is only an experiment that happened to work for long enough. When I change a joint my grandfather used, I am not betraying him; I am doing exactly what he did when he changed his father's."

Teodor Brisk, town planner: "Every generation believes it has finally learned how to live. We pull down the old covered market because it looks inefficient, and twenty years later we pay consultants to design something that feels just like it."

Amara Holt, engineer: "Progress is not a direction; it is a measurement. Unless you can say what has become better, and for whom, the word is only a compliment we pay to whatever is new."

Lise Marand, archivist: "We should not keep old customs merely because they are old, but we should keep a careful record of them. A method abandoned today may be the answer to a problem nobody has had yet."
items.question: Which speaker suggests that changing a tradition can itself be a way of continuing it?

options.text: Teodor Brisk
Amara Holt
Orla Vance
Lise Marand

B Holt는 진보를 측정 기준으로 정의할 뿐 전통의 계승을 말하지 않는다. D Marand는 옛 방식을 '기록'으로 남기자고 할 뿐 바꾸는 것이 계승이라고 하지 않는다. 유형 팁: 인용문 문항은 선택지의 핵심어를 각 화자의 문장과 하나씩 대조하라. → 정답 C

items.stimulus:
Two editors at a regional newspaper discuss whether to name a man who has been arrested.

Rhea: The police have arrested the deputy treasurer of Halvern Council over missing funds. A rival station has already named him online. If we stay silent, readers will simply get the name from someone less careful than us.

Tomas: Being second to a name is not a cost I lose sleep over. Being wrong about one is. He has been arrested, not charged. Plenty of people are released without any charge at all.

Rhea: I'm not proposing we call him guilty. We would report exactly what is true: that he was arrested and questioned. The public pays his salary, so they have a stronger claim to know than they would for a private citizen.

Tomas: The facts may be true, but readers don't hear them neutrally. Ask anyone in six months and they'll remember 'the treasurer and the fraud', not the word 'arrested'. Our accuracy doesn't protect him from that.

Rhea: Then our job is to explain the difference, not to hide the information. Treating readers as if they can't tell an arrest from a conviction is its own kind of disrespect.

Tomas: Perhaps. But think about what happens if he is released next week. Will we give that story the front page too?

Rhea: We should, and I'd commit to it now.

Tomas: Then write that commitment into our policy before we name anyone, and I'll reconsider. Until then, we report the arrest of 'a council official' and nothing more.
items.question: Tomas's main concern about naming the man is that

options.text: the rival station's report may contain factual errors.
readers are likely to remember an arrest as if it implied guilt.

items.stimulus:
Modern audiences often assume that a mask hides an actor. In many theatrical traditions, its purpose was closer to the opposite: it was meant to reveal a type, a force or a feeling more clearly than an ordinary face could. In the large open-air theatres of ancient Greece, spectators far from the stage could not have read small changes in an actor's expression. A mask with bold features made a character recognisable at a distance, and it allowed a small company of actors to play many roles.

Some traditions treat the mask as fixed in meaning yet flexible in use. In Japanese Noh theatre, a carved mask may seem to brighten or darken as the performer tilts it slightly towards or away from the light, so that a single unchanging object carries a range of emotions. The skill lies less in the mask than in how precisely the body around it moves. Performers in the Italian commedia dell'arte wore half-masks that identified stock characters, such as the greedy merchant or the boastful soldier. Audiences knew within seconds what to expect from each, which left the actors free to improvise.

A further function is harder to describe in theatrical terms. In a number of ritual performances, a masked performer is understood not to be portraying a spirit or ancestor but, for the length of the performance, to be one. Here the mask does not represent an absent being; it makes that being present. To call such a performer an 'actor' at all may bring in a distinction between pretending and being that the participants themselves do not draw.

What these cases share is that the mask removes the individual performer's personality from view. The audience is invited to attend not to who is performing but to what is being performed.

items.stimulus:
Tipping is often defended as a way of rewarding good service. In practice, it does a poor job of that and a good job of several things nobody would choose deliberately. Restaurants should abolish it and pay staff a wage that already includes what tips are supposed to provide.

Consider first what a tip actually measures. Studies of restaurant tipping have repeatedly found that the size of a tip is only weakly related to how diners rate the service they received. Tips vary far more with the size of the bill, the weather, the mood of the customer and whether the server happened to introduce themselves by name. A system that claims to reward quality but mostly rewards luck is not a merit system; it is a lottery with a polite name.

Second, tipping moves part of the cost of running the business from the owner to the customer, while keeping it out of sight. The menu price looks lower than the real price, which flatters the restaurant and misleads the diner. Almost every other trade puts its labour costs on the price tag. A plumber does not invite you to decide, after the pipe is fixed, how much his apprentice deserves to earn this week.

Third, depending on tips makes workers' incomes unpredictable. A server who earns well on a busy Saturday may earn little on a wet Tuesday, with no difference in effort. People who rely on tips find it harder to plan, to borrow and to save.

Defenders of tipping warn that without it, service will decline, because staff will no longer have a reason to try. But this assumes that the only thing that makes people work well is the hope of an immediate cash reward from a stranger. Nurses, teachers and pilots are not tipped, and we do not conclude that they therefore have no reason to do their jobs properly.

Some restaurants that have dropped tipping have raised their menu prices and lost customers, at least at first. That is an argument for making the change together, through a clear industry standard, rather than an argument for keeping a system that serves almost no one well.

items.stimulus:
Every map is a set of decisions about what to leave out. A map that showed everything at its true size would have to be as large as the land itself, and it would be useless for the same reason. Mapmakers therefore practise what they call generalisation: the deliberate simplification of the world so that a map can serve its purpose at its scale.

Generalisation takes several forms. Selection decides which features appear at all: a national road map may show motorways and main roads but leave out lanes and footpaths. Simplification smooths the details of a feature that remains, so that a coastline with thousands of small inlets becomes a line with a few broad curves. Exaggeration enlarges features that matter but would otherwise vanish; a road drawn at its true width on a 1 : 1,000,000 map would be thinner than a human hair, so it is drawn many times wider than it really is. Displacement then moves neighbouring features apart, because a widened road would otherwise overlap the railway that runs beside it.

None of these operations is neutral. Each is guided by what the map is for and who will use it. A walking map of a mountain area will keep a narrow path and a small spring that a motoring atlas would leave out, while dropping petrol stations that the atlas would show clearly. The same valley, mapped twice, can look like two different places.

This dependence on purpose means that the most useful map is rarely the most detailed one. Experiments with map readers have found that adding features beyond what a task requires tends to slow people down and increase errors, because the relevant information is harder to pick out. A good map, in this sense, is defined as much by what it leaves out as by what it contains.

Generalisation also raises questions of trust. Readers usually cannot see what has been removed, so they may take a simplified map for a complete one. A village left off a regional map has not vanished, but a reader who does not know the area has no way of knowing it was ever there. For this reason, some mapmakers argue that maps should state the purpose for which they were generalised, so that readers can judge what kinds of omission to expect.

Every map is a set of decisions about what to leave out. A map that showed everything at its true size would have to be as large as the land itself, and it would be useless for the same reason. Mapmakers therefore practise what they call generalisation: the deliberate simplification of the world so that a map can serve its purpose at its scale.

Generalisation takes several forms. Selection decides which features appear at all: a national road map may show motorways and main roads but leave out lanes and footpaths. Simplification smooths the details of a feature that remains, so that a coastline with thousands of small inlets becomes a line with a few broad curves. Exaggeration enlarges features that matter but would otherwise vanish; a road drawn at its true width on a 1 : 1,000,000 map would be thinner than a human hair, so it is drawn many times wider than it really is. Displacement then moves neighbouring features apart, because a widened road would otherwise overlap the railway that runs beside it.

None of these operations is neutral. Each is guided by what the map is for and who will use it. A walking map of a mountain area will keep a narrow path and a small spring that a motoring atlas would leave out, while dropping petrol stations that the atlas would show clearly. The same valley, mapped twice, can look like two different places.

This dependence on purpose means that the most useful map is rarely the most detailed one. Experiments with map readers have found that adding features beyond what a task requires tends to slow people down and increase errors, because the relevant information is harder to pick out. A good map, in this sense, is defined as much by what it leaves out as by what it contains.

Generalisation also raises questions of trust. Readers usually cannot see what has been removed, so they may take a simplified map for a complete one. A village left off a regional map has not vanished, but a reader who does not know the area has no way of knowing it was ever there. For this reason, some mapmakers argue that maps should state the purpose for which they were generalised, so that readers can judge what kinds of omission to expect.

items.stimulus:
Most moral traditions agree that it is wrong to harm an innocent person in order to achieve a good end. Yet many also accept that a good action may sometimes be allowed even though it is known to cause harm as a side-effect. The doctrine of double effect, whose origins are usually traced to medieval discussions of self-defence, tries to explain where the line lies.

In its common form, the doctrine allows an action with both a good and a bad effect only if four conditions are met. The action must not be wrong in itself. The person acting must intend only the good effect, not the bad one. The bad effect must not be the means by which the good effect is achieved. And there must be a serious enough reason to accept the bad effect, so that the good clearly outweighs it.

Consider an engineer who must release water from a dam that is about to fail. If she opens the spillway, a farm downstream will be flooded, but the town below the dam will be saved. On the doctrine's view, she may open it: the flooding is foreseen, but it is not her aim, and the town is saved by relieving pressure on the dam, not by flooding the farm. Compare an official who floods the same farm deliberately so that its owner, fearing further damage, will finally sell the land needed for a flood barrier. Here the harm is the very means by which the official pursues his goal, and the doctrine forbids it, even if the barrier would protect thousands of people.

Critics argue that the difference between intending and merely foreseeing is too thin to carry moral weight. The farmer's fields are equally underwater in both cases; why should what is in someone's mind make the difference between right and wrong? Defenders reply that the doctrine is not mainly about outcomes but about what kind of agent one becomes. A person who uses another's loss as a tool has made that loss part of her plan, and that, they say, is a different kind of act.

items.stimulus:
For most of history, extinction has been final. Advances in genetic engineering have begun to blur that boundary. Some scientists now propose to create animals resembling extinct species, such as the woolly mammoth, by editing the genes of their closest living relatives. Supporters call this 'de-extinction'. Whether it should be attempted is as much an ethical question as a technical one.

The strongest case for de-extinction rests on responsibility. Many species disappeared because of human hunting or the destruction of their habitats. If we caused the loss, the argument goes, and we can now repair it, we have at least a reason to try. Supporters add that some revived species might restore ecological roles that have been missing for centuries, such as large grazing animals that once kept grasslands open.

Critics raise three concerns. First, the animal produced would not be the species that was lost but a new creature engineered to resemble it. It would lack the learned behaviours that its ancestors passed between generations, and it would have no wild population to learn from. Second, the money and attention spent on reviving the dead may be drawn away from protecting species that are still alive but threatened. A government that funds a mammoth may feel less pressure to fund the protection of a living elephant. Third, the habitats in which extinct animals once lived have often changed or disappeared, so a revived animal may have nowhere suitable to live.

These objections do not all point the same way. The first asks whether de-extinction can achieve what it promises; the second asks whether it is the best use of limited resources; the third asks whether the world is ready to receive what it would create. A project might answer one objection and still fail the others. The real question, then, is not whether bringing back a lost species would be good in principle, but whether a particular project can show that it would do more good than the same effort spent on the living.

items.stimulus:
For most of history, extinction has been final. Advances in genetic engineering have begun to blur that boundary. Some scientists now propose to create animals resembling extinct species, such as the woolly mammoth, by editing the genes of their closest living relatives. Supporters call this 'de-extinction'. Whether it should be attempted is as much an ethical question as a technical one.

The strongest case for de-extinction rests on responsibility. Many species disappeared because of human hunting or the destruction of their habitats. If we caused the loss, the argument goes, and we can now repair it, we have at least a reason to try. Supporters add that some revived species might restore ecological roles that have been missing for centuries, such as large grazing animals that once kept grasslands open.

Critics raise three concerns. First, the animal produced would not be the species that was lost but a new creature engineered to resemble it. It would lack the learned behaviours that its ancestors passed between generations, and it would have no wild population to learn from. Second, the money and attention spent on reviving the dead may be drawn away from protecting species that are still alive but threatened. A government that funds a mammoth may feel less pressure to fund the protection of a living elephant. Third, the habitats in which extinct animals once lived have often changed or disappeared, so a revived animal may have nowhere suitable to live.

These objections do not all point the same way. The first asks whether de-extinction can achieve what it promises; the second asks whether it is the best use of limited resources; the third asks whether the world is ready to receive what it would create. A project might answer one objection and still fail the others. The real question, then, is not whether bringing back a lost species would be good in principle, but whether a particular project can show that it would do more good than the same effort spent on the living.

The regional town of Hallam Creek is running a two-year pilot in which 500 adult residents each receive $300 a week, with no conditions attached. Four people give their views.

items.stimulus:
The story of the Dutch 'tulip mania' of the 1630s is one of the most retold episodes in economic history. In the popular version, ordinary people across the Dutch Republic sold houses and land to buy single tulip bulbs, prices rose to absurd heights, and when the market crashed in early 1637, the country was thrown into ruin. Much of this version reached modern readers through a widely read book published in 1841 by the Scottish writer Charles Mackay, two centuries after the events.

Historians who have examined surviving contracts drawn up by notaries, court records and town archives have found a more modest picture. Prices for rare bulbs did rise sharply over the winter of 1636-37 and then collapsed in February 1637; on that point the records and the legend agree. But the buyers named in the documents were mostly merchants, craftsmen and other people of reasonable means, not the poor. Much of the trading took place in taverns, through contracts for bulbs that were still in the ground, so money often never changed hands before the collapse. When prices fell, many buyers simply refused to honour these contracts, and the disputes were often settled for a fraction of the agreed price.

Nor do the archives show the wave of bankruptcies that the legend describes. Researchers searching for people ruined by tulips have found few clear cases, and the Dutch economy of the period continued to grow.

Why, then, did the dramatic version last? Part of the answer is that some of its most vivid details came from moralising pamphlets printed at the time, which used the tulip trade to warn against greed and vanity. items.stimulus:
The story of the Dutch 'tulip mania' of the 1630s is one of the most retold episodes in economic history. In the popular version, ordinary people across the Dutch Republic sold houses and land to buy single tulip bulbs, prices rose to absurd heights, and when the market crashed in early 1637, the country was thrown into ruin. Historians who have examined surviving contracts drawn up by notaries, court records and town archives have found a more modest picture. Prices for rare bulbs did rise sharply over the winter of 1636-37 and then collapsed in February 1637; on that point the records and the legend agree. When prices fell, many buyers simply refused to honour these contracts, and the disputes were often settled for a fraction of the agreed price.

Why, then, did the dramatic version last? Part of the answer is that some of its most vivid details came from moralising pamphlets printed at the time, which used the tulip trade to warn against greed and vanity. These pamphlets were never meant as neutral reports. Later writers, finding them colourful and easy to quote, treated them as evidence.

items.question: In a town election, the Riverside Alliance won 32% of the vote in 2018 and 40% of the vote in 2022. By what percentage did its share of the vote increase, relative to its 2018 share?
items.explanation_ko: 1) 증가분 40 - 32 = 8퍼센트포인트. 2) 처음 값 대비 증가율 8 / 32 = 1/4 = 25%. 오답: A 8%는 퍼센트포인트 차이를 퍼센트 증가율로 착각한 값이다. B 20%는 나중 값(40)을 분모로 쓴 값이다. D 40%는 2022년 득표율 자체다. 유형 팁: '퍼센트포인트'와 '퍼센트 증가율'을 구분하고 분모는 처음 값을 쓴다. → 정답 C
